meta.description: Paintings influenced by, or critically connected to, Claude Monet's Water Lilies (Les Nymphéas). Intended as edge targets for a d3/React visualization whose source catalog is water_lilies_catalog.json. Monet painting IDs use the Wildenstein catalogue raisonné numbers (e.g. W.1973) present in water_lilies_catalog.json's `catalog_number` field; Orangerie panels use the 'First room: N' / 'Second room: N' keys from the same file.
meta.image_url_note: Where a stable museum or Wikimedia image URL was known it is used. Where not, the string is set to 'PLACEHOLDER' so you can drop in a URL manually. image_source_page always points to a canonical attribution page.

image_rights_legend.public_domain: Work is out of copyright; reproduction rights generally free.
image_rights_legend.copyright_estate: Under artist-estate copyright; require license for non-editorial use.
image_rights_legend.fair_use_educational: Reproducing under U.S. fair-use / educational exemption at small size.

connection_type_legend.all-over: Compositional evenness, no figure/ground hierarchy (Greenberg's Monet→Pollock argument).
connection_type_legend.horizonless: No anchoring horizon line; the pond-surface trick abstracted.
connection_type_legend.scale-immersive: Room-filling canvases that envelop the viewer (Grandes Décorations → Rothko Chapel, Newman).
connection_type_legend.color-field: Large expanses of modulated color doing the expressive work.
connection_type_legend.direct-homage: Artist explicitly quotes the Water Lilies motif.
connection_type_legend.biographical: Artist lived near Giverny / visited the pond / knew Monet's circle.
connection_type_legend.loose-critical: Typological or retrospective critical link only.

connection_strength_legend.direct: Artist said it (letters, interviews, studio statements).
connection_strength_legend.documented: Scholar or curator has proved it with archival evidence.
connection_strength_legend.critical: Critic or curator drew the link at the time or since.
connection_strength_legend.loose: Typological resemblance only; no documentary chain.

paintings.title: Autumn Rhythm (Number 30)
paintings.connection_claim: Clement Greenberg's 1956 essay 'The Later Monet' argued that Pollock's all-over, horizonless webs continue the pictorial logic of Monet's late Water Lilies; Alfred Barr's acquisition and installation of Monet's triptych at MoMA (W.1973) was staged to make that lineage visible alongside Pollock.
paintings.citation: Clement Greenberg, 'The Later Monet,' Art News Annual 26 (1957), 132–148.

paintings.title: No. 14, 1960
paintings.connection_claim: Curators and critics from William Seitz (MoMA 1960) onward read Rothko's wall-scaled color envelopes as the post-war American analogue of the Orangerie's curved, room-sized immersion — the viewer is placed inside color rather than in front of an image.
paintings.citation: William C. Seitz, Monet: Seasons and Moments, exh. cat. (New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 1960).

paintings.title: Rothko Chapel, North Apse Triptych
paintings.medium: oil and mixed media on canvas
paintings.dimensions: central panel 457.2 × 304.8 cm; flanking panels each c. 335.3 × 243.8 cm
paintings.connection_claim: The Rothko Chapel is routinely read as a non-denominational American descendant of the Orangerie's two oval rooms: a site-specific, purpose-built environment whose meaning is produced by wrapping the spectator in a continuous field of painted color.
paintings.citation: Robert Rosenblum, Modern Painting and the Northern Romantic Tradition: Friedrich to Rothko (Harper & Row, 1975), chapter 7.

paintings.title: Vir Heroicus Sublimis
paintings.connection_claim: Newman's instruction — 'There is a tendency to look at large pictures from a distance. The large pictures in this exhibition are intended to be seen from a short distance.' — codifies the same immersive, peripheral-vision experience Monet engineered at the Orangerie: the canvas is a field the viewer stands inside, not a window.
paintings.citation: Barnett Newman, wall statement for his second exhibition at Betty Parsons Gallery, April 1951; reprinted in John P. O'Neill (ed.), Barnett Newman: Selected Writings and Interviews (Knopf, 1990), 178.

paintings.title: La Grande Vallée XIV (For a Little While)
paintings.connection_claim: Mitchell lived from 1968 until her death in the house at Vétheuil on the hillside above Monet's earlier property; her late multi-panel landscapes, and the Grande Vallée cycle in particular, were read by curators (most explicitly in the 2022 Fondation Louis Vuitton 'Monet–Mitchell' pairing) as a direct, lived continuation of Monet's Grandes Décorations.
paintings.citation: Suzanne Pagé and Angela Lampe (eds.), Monet–Mitchell, exh. cat. (Paris: Fondation Louis Vuitton / Hazan, 2022).

paintings.title: Mountains and Sea
paintings.medium: oil and charcoal on unprimed canvas
paintings.connection_claim: Frankenthaler's soak-stain technique — pigment soaking into unprimed canvas so that image and support are one membrane — was read by Greenberg and Michael Fried as the American crystallisation of the optical indeterminacy of Monet's late pond paintings, where water, reflection, and painted surface collapse into a single field.
paintings.citation: Michael Fried, 'Morris Louis,' in Art and Objecthood (University of Chicago Press, 1998), 102–121; orig. 1967.

paintings.title: Tet
paintings.connection_claim: The Veil paintings' translucent overlaid washes were framed by Greenberg and later by John Elderfield as the most disciplined inheritance of Monet's submerged greens at the Orangerie: pigment is no longer on the canvas, it is the canvas, just as Monet's water had no surface.
paintings.citation: John Elderfield, Morris Louis, exh. cat. (New York: The Museum of Modern Art, 1986).

paintings.title: Towards Disappearance II
paintings.connection_claim: Sam Francis, living in Paris through the 1950s and working at mural scale, repeatedly cited the Orangerie as the decisive modern precedent; Peter Selz framed his white-centred, edge-gathered compositions as Francis's version of Monet's pond — emptiness in the middle, colour-event at the periphery.
paintings.citation: Peter Selz, Sam Francis (New York: Harry N. Abrams, 1975; rev. ed. 1982).

paintings.title: Dial
paintings.connection_claim: The term 'Abstract Impressionism' was coined by Louis Finkelstein in 1956 precisely to describe Guston's pulsing, centre-weighted dabs of pink, red and grey — paint behaving like the late Monet's chromatic haze, without Pollock's drawn linearity.

paintings.title: Untitled V
paintings.connection_claim: De Kooning's late-1970s 'pastoral' paintings, made in East Hampton on canvases mixed with water, safflower oil and kerosene to stay wet for weeks, were identified by curators including Diane Waldman and later Richard Shiff as his explicit attempt to regain Monet's watery, weather-soaked palette.
paintings.citation: Richard Shiff, Between Sense and de Kooning (Reaktion Books, 2011), 142–167.

paintings.title: Tableau Vert
paintings.connection_claim: Kelly visited Giverny in 1952, while living in France, and found Monet's then-dust-covered late panels in the abandoned Atelier des Nymphéas; Tableau Vert — a single modulated green rectangle — is documented by Kelly himself as a direct response to that encounter, painted within weeks of his visit.
paintings.citation: Yve-Alain Bois, Ellsworth Kelly: The Years in France, 1948–1954, exh. cat. (Washington, D.C.: National Gallery of Art, 1992).

paintings.title: Water Lilies with Japanese Bridge
paintings.medium: enamel on processed and swirled stainless steel
paintings.connection_claim: Lichtenstein's Water Lilies series of 1992 reproduces the Japanese Footbridge compositions in Ben-Day dots and printed stainless steel — an explicitly parodic homage that also re-reads Monet's surface as already a printed, reproducible sign.
paintings.citation: Roy Lichtenstein, interview with Michael Kimmelman, The New York Times, October 9, 1992, 'At the Met with Roy Lichtenstein: Monet? Rodin? Roy Likes Them Best in the Morning.'

paintings.title: Quattro Stagioni: Primavera
paintings.medium: acrylic, oil, crayon and pencil on canvas
paintings.connection_claim: Twombly's Quattro Stagioni — seasonal cycles of dripped crimson, green and ochre — were framed by Richard Leeman and by the Tate curators as late-modernist seasonal pendants to Monet's year-long pond observations, cycles of dissolution rather than landscapes.
paintings.citation: Richard Leeman, Cy Twombly: A Monograph (Thames & Hudson, 2005), 242–260.

paintings.title: Cold Mountain 6 (Bridge)
paintings.connection_claim: Gary Garrels and Richard Shiff both described Marden's calligraphic, looping Cold Mountain paintings as a late-twentieth-century equivalent of Monet's late Japanese Footbridge canvases — an abstraction derived from arboreal, reflected line rather than from grid or geometry.
paintings.citation: Gary Garrels (ed.), Plane Image: A Brice Marden Retrospective, exh. cat. (New York: MoMA, 2006).

paintings.title: Genie
paintings.connection_claim: Resnick is the other painter named by Finkelstein in the 1956 'Abstract-Impressionism' essay; his late-1950s paintings are dense, edge-to-edge crusts of broken colour that critics repeatedly described as post-war Nymphéas in thicker paint.

paintings.title: PH-950 (1950-A No. 2)
paintings.connection_claim: Still rejected European precedents and specifically refused the Monet comparison, but curators from Dean Sobel onward have noted typological proximity: wall-height, horizonless fields of modulated single colour punctured by thin tears — the same bodily-scale proposition as the Orangerie.
paintings.citation: Dean Sobel and David Anfam, Clyfford Still: The Artist's Museum (Skira Rizzoli, 2012).

paintings.title: Seestück (See-See)
paintings.connection_claim: Richter's Seestücke splice two photographs of water into a horizonless mirror; Dietmar Elger and Benjamin Buchloh both invoked late Monet as the obvious nineteenth-century precedent for a painting whose only subject is the optical impossibility of water meeting water.
paintings.citation: Dietmar Elger, Gerhard Richter: A Life in Painting (University of Chicago Press, 2009), 180–194.

paintings.title: Waterfall
paintings.connection_claim: Steir has repeatedly named Monet as a primary reference and credits the Orangerie with her decision to let gravity and dilution — not drawing — carry the image; her poured Waterfalls restage the late Nymphéas' subject (water falling through water) as process.
paintings.citation: Pat Steir, in conversation with Anne Waldman, BOMB Magazine 83 (Spring 2003).

paintings.title: Architecture of the Sky III
paintings.connection_claim: Bleckner's dark, dotted, light-pierced fields were read by Lisa Phillips and others as late-twentieth-century sky-versions of Monet's cloud-reflection panels at the Orangerie — the same device (suspended points of illumination on a dark chromatic ground) transposed from water to sky.
paintings.citation: Lisa Phillips, Ross Bleckner, exh. cat. (New York: Guggenheim Museum, 1995).
